results.claim: Fixed-placement feasibility has an exact matching characterization, yielding an XP exact algorithm parameterized by the number k of bugs.
results.proof_sketch: Fix t≤k labeled bugs and their host multiset. For every safe house v, let A(v) be the bugs hosted in N[v]. Form a bipartite graph with the safe houses on the left and all nonempty subsets of the t bugs on the right, joining v to S exactly when S⊆A(v). A matching saturating the safe-house side assigns distinct nonempty feasible signatures. Conversely, any feasible signature assignment gives such a matching and defines monitored sets M(b)={v:b∈S(v)}⊆N[host(b)]. Thus fixed-placement feasibility is exactly matching feasibility. Enumerating, for every t≤k, the binomial(n+t−1,t) host multisets and applying this test decides OPT≤k in f(k)n^{k+O(1)} time, which is XP.

results.claim: Regional information bound: for every X⊆V, at least ceil(log2(|X|+1)) bugs must be hosted in N[X]. Moreover, the optimum is additive over connected components.
results.proof_sketch: Every signature of a vertex in X uses only bugs whose hosts lie in N[X]=union_{x∈X}N[x]. If h bugs are hosted there, only 2^h−1 nonempty subsets of those bugs exist, so |X|≤2^h−1. If several sets X_i have pairwise disjoint N[X_i], their bounds add. For components, no bug can hear across components, so restricting any solution to each component gives a solution there. Conversely, componentwise solutions can be united: their bug sets are disjoint, and nonempty signatures from different components therefore cannot coincide. Hence OPT(G)=sum_C OPT(C).

results.claim: If every connected component C has a universal safe house, then OPT is exactly sum_C ceil(log2(|C|+1)), computable in polynomial time.
results.proof_sketch: The information bound applied to a component C gives OPT(C)≥ceil(log2(|C|+1)). If u is universal in C, put that many bugs at u. Every safe house can hear all of them, so assign the |C| houses arbitrary distinct nonempty subsets. This attains the lower bound. Component additivity proves the formula. Components and universal vertices can be found in polynomial time.

results.claim: Incidence-capacity lower bound: if rho=max_v |N[v]| and a solution has k bugs, then L(n,k)≤k rho, where L(n,k) is the minimum total cardinality of n distinct nonempty subsets of a k-element set.
results.proof_sketch: Let the signatures be S(v). Double-count incidences: sum_v |S(v)|=sum_b |M(b)|. A bug hosted at z monitors only a subset of N[z], so the right side is at most k rho. The left side is minimized by filling subset-cardinality layers in increasing order. Explicitly, if s is least with sum_{j=1}^s binomial(k,j)≥n, then L(n,k)=sum_{j=1}^{s−1}j binomial(k,j)+s(n−sum_{j=1}^{s−1}binomial(k,j)). In particular, at most k signatures are singletons, so L(n,k)≥2n−k.

results.claim: The problem is exactly solvable on interval graphs of maximum degree at most two. For every connected component C of order n, OPT(C)=floor(n/2)+1; componentwise summation gives the general answer.
results.proof_sketch: A connected maximum-degree-two graph is a path or cycle. An interval graph has no induced cycle of length at least four: choosing a cycle interval with minimum right endpoint makes its two cycle neighbors meet at that endpoint, creating a chord. Thus each component is a path or K3; the universal-vertex formula gives OPT(K3)=2. For P_n, each bug occurs in at most three signatures, while distinctness gives sum_v|S(v)|≥2n−k. Hence k≥ceil(n/2). If n=2t and k=t, equality forces exactly t singleton and t pair signatures, while every bug must monitor all three vertices around an internal host. Bugs with the same host would occur together on three vertices, producing duplicate pair codes; bugs at adjacent hosts would occur together on their two common vertices, again producing duplicate pair codes. Thus the t hosts must be distinct, nonadjacent internal vertices, but P_{2t} has room for only t−1, a contradiction. Hence k≥t+1. For P_{2t+1}, host bugs at vertices 1,3,…,2t+1, give each odd vertex its singleton, and each even vertex the pair from its adjacent hosts. For P_{2t}, use the analogous odd hosts and add one bug at vertex 2t, giving the final vertex its new singleton. These constructions use floor(n/2)+1 bugs.

results.claim: Running the source greedy algorithm in both timeline directions and taking the better result is not exact, even on a connected symmetric instance: both runs use seven bugs while OPT=6.
results.proof_sketch: Take L1=[−2/5,0], L2=[−2/5,1], L3=[3/5,2], L4=[8/5,3], L5=[8/5,4], L6=[13/5,5], U=[7/2,23/2], and let Ri be the reflection of Li under x↦15−x. The family is reflection-invariant. Its left chain meets U through L6, U meets R6, and the reflected chain completes a connected intersection graph. The forward timeline order is L1,L2,L3,L4,L5,L6,U,R6,R4,R5,R3,R1,R2. Exact execution adds bugs at processing/host positions (1,2),(2,3),(4,6),(6,7),(9,11),(11,13),(13,13); reflection gives the same seven events in the reverse run. Six bugs suffice: host a,b,c at L2,L3,L5 and d,e,f at R5,R3,R2. Give L1,…,L6 codes {a},{a,b},{a,b,c},{b},{b,c},{c}; give R1,…,R6 codes {f},{e,f},{d,e,f},{e},{d,e},{d}; and give U code {c,d}. These thirteen codes are feasible, nonempty, and distinct. For X_L={L1,…,L4}, N[X_L]={L1,…,L6}; symmetrically, X_R={R1,…,R4} has N[X_R]={R1,…,R6}. The neighborhoods are disjoint, and each four-vertex region requires at least ceil(log2(5))=3 hosted bugs. Therefore OPT≥6, proving OPT=6.

results.claim: The decision problem parameterized by the bug budget k is fixed-parameter tractable: OPT≤k can be decided in 2^{O(k^2)} times a polynomial in the input size.
results.proof_sketch: Any system using at most k bugs supplies at most 2^k−1 distinct nonempty signatures. Thus an instance with n>2^k−1 vertices is immediately a NO-instance. Otherwise enumerate, for every t≤k, all n^t labeled t-bug host placements. There are at most (k+1)(2^k−1)^k=2^{O(k^2)} such placements. For each placement, apply the fixed-placement matching characterization; its right side has at most 2^t−1≤2^k−1 vertices, so the matching test takes 2^{O(k)} times a polynomial in the input size. The total running time is therefore 2^{O(k^2)} times a polynomial in the input size.

final_writeup:
The general approximation threshold remains unresolved. I obtain neither a polynomial-time approximation with ratio strictly below 2 for arbitrary interval families nor an appropriate matching inapproximability theorem. The claimed resolution therefore remains PARTIAL, agreeing with the audit’s VALID_PARTIAL_PROGRESS and ACCURATE judgments.

All six audited claims are retained with their exact claim wording. Fixed-placement feasibility is characterized by bipartite matching; the regional and incidence-capacity inequalities provide lower bounds; components with universal safe houses and interval graphs of maximum degree at most two admit exact formulas; and the symmetric 13-interval construction shows that taking the better of the source greedy algorithm in the two timeline directions is not exact.

Adversarial self-critique yields one additional consequence. The global signature bound upgrades the placement-enumeration algorithm from merely XP to FPT with respect to the bug budget k: a YES-instance has n≤2^k−1, after which all placements and their matching tests take 2^{O(k^2)} times a polynomial in the input size. This exact parameterized result does not settle the requested approximation threshold because k is unrestricted and may grow with the instance.

The 13-interval witness likewise establishes only a 7-versus-6 failure of exactness, a ratio of 7/6. It supplies neither a uniform (2−epsilon)-approximation nor a hardness barrier. A complete resolution still requires one of those two results for arbitrary interval families.
